title: When Is a Graph a Covariance? Bayesian Residual Propagation under Covariance Uncertainty

paper.title: When Is a Graph a Covariance? Bayesian Residual Propagation under Covariance Uncertainty
paper.abstract: Abstract Observing a prediction error at one node can help correct predictions elsewhere, but the benefit depends on the residual dependence between nodes. A graph suggests where that dependence might occur, yet does not establish its sign or strength. We develop a Bayesian model of residual covariance to determine how revealed errors should update a fixed feature-based predictor. For a fixed set of revealed nodes, we derive an exact identity for the change in expected squared error under linear residual propagation. The identity characterizes the optimal linear update and expresses the excess error of any other update as an exact quadratic. Under covariance uncertainty, the Bayes-optimal fixed linear update uses the posterior mean covariance. We average over four positive-semidefinite covariance families representing no dependence, positive dependence, negative dependence, and dependence whose sign can alternate with graph distance. Across eight graph benchmarks, four show posterior support within the distance-profile family for negative covariance between neighbors and alternating signs with distance. Among the evaluated methods, ours achieves the smallest worst-case recall gap to the best method on each graph. The method improves squared error over residual propagation on five of eight graphs, but performs substantially worse on one dense heterophilous graph. In these experiments, selecting the highest-posterior family performs similarly to model averaging.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: We consider prediction on a graph when a feature-based predictor is available and only some node labels can be observed. For each query, the task is to predict which nodes are relevant. Each observed label reveals a prediction error that may help correct predictions at other nodes. An error at one node may call for an adjustment in the same direction elsewhere, an adjustment in the opposite direction, or no adjustment. The graph alone does not tell us which response is appropriate or how large the adjustment should be. We use the graph to construct candidate models of residual covariance, allowing positive, negative, and sign-changing dependence. We learn a posterior over these models from previously labelled queries. For a new query, the resulting covariance estimate guides both the selection of nodes for labelling and the updates to predictions after their labels are observed.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: First, for centred residuals and a fixed set of revealed nodes, we derive an exact identity for the reduction in expected squared error under linear propagation. The identity gives the optimal linear update and expresses the excess error of any other update as an exact quadratic. For a single revealed node, any nonzero adjustment increases expected error when the true residual covariance with the target node is zero. A positive propagation coefficient also increases expected squared error when that covariance is negative. Second, we derive a Bayesian rule for propagation when the residual covariance is unknown. Under expected squared-error loss, the optimal linear rule with coefficients fixed before observing the new labels uses the posterior mean residual covariance. For a single reveal, the adjustment coefficient is zero exactly when the posterior mean cross-covariance is zero, so no separate threshold is needed to turn propagation off. Third, we construct four positive-semidefinite covariance families representing no residual dependence, positive dependence, negative dependence, and dependence whose sign can alternate with graph distance. Proposition 1 shows that the standard Laplacian covariance model considered here has nonnegative covariance entries and nonnegative propagation coefficients. It therefore cannot represent negative residual covariance or covariance that alternates in sign with graph distance. We evaluate the resulting propagation decisions on eight graph benchmarks with varying levels of homophily.

sections.heading: 1.1 Relation to prior work
sections.text: Our work builds on residual propagation and methods for learning on heterophilous graphs.

sections.heading: Residual propagation.
sections.text: Previous work has shown that residuals from feature-based predictors can retain graph structure and that propagating these residuals can improve predictions. Jia and Benson (2020) model GNN regression residuals with a graph-structured Gaussian distribution and estimate a signed dependence parameter by marginal likelihood. Their full model therefore allows both positive and negative residual correlation. Their lightweight LP-GNN variant and the correction step of Huang et al. (2021) assume positive residual dependence. Our experiments include Laplacian propagation and the correction step of Huang et al. (2021) as baselines. They do not include Jia and Benson’s learned signed model. Our method instead places a posterior over several covariance families, including a null model and a distance-based family that permits uniformly negative or alternating covariance across positive graph distances. We hold the feature-based predictor fixed and use the inferred covariance to update its predictions.

sections.heading: Heterophily and selective propagation.
sections.text: Methods that encourage neighbouring nodes to agree can perform poorly on heterophilous graphs, where connected nodes often have different labels ( Pei et al., 2020 ; Zhu et al., 2020 ; Lim et al., 2021 ) . Choi et al. (2025) address uncertainty about edges with an adaptive method that can block propagation. Other methods allow propagation to adapt to the graph: FAGCN combines low- and high-frequency components using weights that can be negative ( Bo et al., 2021 ) , while GPR-GNN learns signed polynomial coefficients ( Chien et al., 2021 ) . These two methods learn their propagation weights as part of training the predictor. We hold the feature-based predictor fixed and use residuals from previously labelled queries to infer which covariance structures are supported by the data. The resulting posterior determines how newly observed errors update the remaining predictions. Label heterophily alone does not determine the residual dependence that remains after fitting the predictor.

sections.heading: Our distinction.
sections.text: We focus on uncertainty about graph-based residual covariance and its consequences for propagation. The update has the standard Bayes-linear form ( Goldstein and Wooff, 2007 ) . Our risk identity makes explicit how the residual covariance determines its benefit and the cost of using a different linear update. Xu et al. (2010) interpret graph smoothing as kriging and estimate graph-based correlations from observed responses. Borovitskiy et al. (2021) develop Laplacian-based covariance models on graphs. Learning kernels from data also has a substantial literature, including kernel alignment and multiple kernel learning ( Cristianini et al., 2001 ; Gönen and Alpaydın, 2011 ) . We target the covariance of residuals from a cross-fitted predictor ( Chernozhukov et al., 2018 ) and place a posterior over covariance families that allow different signs and distance patterns.

sections.heading: Three questions.
sections.text: We ask whether residual covariance exhibits patterns excluded by positive graph smoothing (Q1), how reliably the posterior distinguishes covariance families and how much that choice matters for prediction (Q2), and whether the resulting decisions improve prediction and ranking (Q3).

sections.heading: Data.
sections.text: We use eight graphs: the citation networks cora and citeseer ( Sen et al., 2008 ) , the WebKB/actor graphs texas , cornell , wisconsin and film ( Pei et al., 2020 ) , and the Wikipedia article networks chameleon and squirrel ( Rozemberczki et al., 2021 ) . Graph sizes range from 183 183 to 7600 7600 nodes, mean degrees from 2.74 2.74 to 76.27 76.27 , and edge homophily from 0.061 0.061 to 0.810 0.810 . For the Wikipedia graphs, we discretise the traffic target into five quantile classes. The Wikipedia graphs have a known source of leakage across splits: nodes can share both a neighbourhood and a target ( Platonov et al., 2023 ) . In our copies, this affects 36 % 36\% of squirrel nodes and 46 % 46\% of chameleon nodes. Their results should be interpreted with this limitation in mind.

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: Each target class defines a query. The initial predictor is a cross-fitted logistic regression on node features, and covariance estimation leaves out the target class. Pools are connected neighbourhoods of up to 200 200 nodes. Every covariance operation is therefore on a matrix of that size, at cost O ⁡ ( 200 3 ) O(200^{3}) , and graph distances are truncated at h ≤ 4 h\leq 4 . We use connected pools because uniform node sampling can remove most graph connections. On cora , uniform samples of this size have mean degree 0.29 0.29 , compared with 3.90 3.90 in the full graph. Methods share the initial predictions, labelled set and budget of B = 20 B=20 additional reveals. Each method selects nodes using its own covariance, except that c&sp uses the nodes selected by gmrf . Methods are evaluated on their remaining unrevealed nodes, so the evaluation sets can differ. Acquisition uses an upper confidence bound (UCB), with an exploration bonus based on diag ( K − K : S ( K S ​ S + τ I ) − 1 K S : ) , \sqrt{\operatorname{diag}\!\left(K-K_{:S}(K_{SS}+\tau I)^{-1}K_{S:}\right)}, where τ = 0.05 \tau=0.05 is the regularisation nugget. The covariance therefore affects both node selection and prediction updates. We report mean squared error on unrevealed nodes and recall@ k k , where k k is the number of relevant items in the pool. This count is unavailable at deployment, so recall@ k k evaluates ranking with an oracle-supplied cutoff. Paired bootstrap intervals resample test pools within each graph. On the three small WebKB graphs, a pool covers most of the giant component. These intervals describe within-graph variability, not replication across independent graphs.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare a feature kernel ( feat ), Laplacian smoothing ( gmrf ), and residual propagation based on Huang et al. (2021) , with autoscale ( c&s ) or without it ( c&sp ). The plain correction step performs better in our setting with only 20 20 reveals per pool, where autoscale amplifies the corrections. We therefore report c&sp as the primary residual-propagation baseline.

sections.heading: 5.1 Residual covariance differs across graph regimes

sections.heading: 5.2 Family identification and decision stability
sections.text: Q2: family selection is sensitive to the likelihood, while selection and averaging give similar predictions under the original likelihood.

sections.heading: Likelihood sensitivity.
sections.text: The likelihood treats residual vectors from different target classes as independent, making it a composite likelihood ( Ribatet et al., 2012 ) . Unadjusted composite likelihoods overcount dependent evidence and concentrate the posterior, which pushes averaging toward the highest-posterior family. An adjustment would need an effective sample size we cannot justify for overlapping pools. Recomputing the evidence with one class per pool, cycling over three choices, changes the selected family on six of eight graphs. Only cora and squirrel retain the same selection. This change reduces both the number of likelihood terms and their dependence, so it does not isolate the effect of dependence alone. Under the reduced likelihoods the averaged covariance is worse on six of eight graphs, by 0.0008 0.0008 in squared error on average. cora and squirrel hold M + M_{+} under every class choice; the graphs selecting M H M_{H} scatter. Under the original likelihood, selecting the highest-posterior family ( map ) and averaging over families ( bayes ) differ by at most 0.0002 0.0002 in squared error and 0.0039 0.0039 in recall. The largest recall difference occurs on citeseer . Similar predictive performance does not imply similar covariance estimates or propagation coefficients.

sections.heading: Recovery of the generating family.
sections.text: We simulate residuals on the cora graph under each covariance family. Gaussian simulations assess selection under a correctly specified model. Thresholding a latent Gaussian produces binary data for a misspecification check. In the binary case, the generating-family label refers to the latent covariance, not necessarily the observed covariance. The recovery table in the supplement reports selection frequencies. The selected family matches the generating label in 73 % 73\% of Gaussian and 77 % 77\% of binary simulations. M + M_{+} is selected in every replicate generated from that family. M − M_{-} is recovered in every Gaussian replicate but is selected as M 0 M_{0} in half of the binary replicates. When M 0 M_{0} generates the data, it is selected in 92 % 92\% and 83 % 83\% of replicates, respectively. In the Gaussian simulations, M H M_{H} is always selected as M + M_{+} . A geometric profile dominated by positive covariance can resemble the positive Laplacian family. These results show that the posterior weights do not reliably distinguish all generating families.

sections.heading: Prediction cost of family selection.
sections.text: The supplement evaluates simulated propagation rules using the oracle regret in Theorem 1 , normalised by the cost of not propagating. Under Gaussian residuals, supplying the generating family reduces normalised regret by 0.008 0.008 relative to averaging, while always using M + M_{+} increases it by 0.323 0.323 . Thus, in these simulations, restricting the available covariance patterns matters more for prediction than knowing the generating family. The binary experiment uses a latent-scale oracle, so its result is a discrepancy diagnostic rather than a fraction of attainable predictive gain.

sections.text: To assess performance across datasets, we measure each method’s recall shortfall from the best method on each graph. bayes has the smallest maximum recall shortfall, 0.0219 0.0219 , followed by map at 0.0225 0.0225 . sections.text: The largest squared-error loss occurs on squirrel , where bayes exceeds c&sp by 0.0125 0.0125 , with paired interval [ 0.0089 , 0.0163 ] [0.0089,0.0163] . The posterior assigns essentially all weight to M + M_{+} . Observed edge covariance is positive, at 0.00060 0.00060 compared with 0.00005 0.00005 off edges, but that sign alone does not establish that M + M_{+} is the best predictive covariance model. prof , the M H M_{H} -only method, has lower test squared error, 0.1402 0.1402 versus 0.1488 0.1488 . Here, marginal likelihood and test squared error favour different families. Family choice can also help. On cora , selecting M + M_{+} raises recall from 0.7495 0.7495 for M H M_{H} alone to 0.7586 0.7586 . The matching performance of map and bayes shows that this gain comes from family choice, with little additional benefit from averaging in these experiments.

sections.heading: 6 Negative Results and Ablations
sections.text: We examined two alternatives. Updating covariance-family weights within a query changed them by at most 0.01 0.01 over B = 20 B=20 reveals. In these experiments, the new observations therefore had little effect on the family weights, as noted in Remark 2 . Finally, evaluating candidate updates with ( 2 ) after substituting an estimated covariance selects the update optimal for that estimate by construction. This criterion selected the plug-in update on all eight graphs. It does not independently assess the covariance estimate, which motivates comparing covariance models through their working likelihoods.

sections.heading: 7 Discussion
sections.text: A graph suggests how prediction errors may be related, but does not establish their covariance. We use a posterior over covariance families to determine how observed errors should update predictions elsewhere. Under the stated assumptions, the posterior mean covariance gives the Bayes-optimal fixed linear update. For a single reveal, the propagation coefficient is zero when the posterior mean cross-covariance is zero, so no separate threshold is needed to turn propagation off. Across eight graphs, model averaging and selecting the highest-posterior family give similar results. Model averaging has the smallest maximum recall shortfall among the methods evaluated. Squared error improves over the residual-propagation baseline on five graphs, but the largest loss exceeds the largest improvement. Several limitations remain. The theory concerns squared error and provides no recall guarantee. Maximum excess squared error is 0.0125 0.0125 for our method, compared with 0.0032 0.0032 for the residual-propagation baseline, with the largest loss on squirrel . Family selection changes on six graphs under the reduced likelihood, and predictive performance under that likelihood has not been evaluated. The simulations also show that distinct covariance families can be difficult to distinguish. The theory assumes fixed reveal sets and centred residuals, while the experiments select adaptively and use a pooled bias correction. Evaluation is limited to eight node-classification benchmarks and four covariance families, with only one near-disjoint training pool on each small WebKB graph. Extending the analysis to adaptive selection and allowing residual dependence to vary across a graph are natural next steps.

sections.text: Each target class is a query. Pools are BFS neighbourhoods of up to 200 200 nodes seeded in the giant component. Uniform node samples are not used. On cora , uniform samples of this size have mean degree 0.29 0.29 , compared with 3.90 3.90 in the full graph, so we use connected pools to retain enough graph structure for the comparison. sections.text: The predictive mean is ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -regularised logistic regression on node features, cross-fitted over 5 5 folds. sections.text: The model evidence factorises as L m ​ ( θ , 𝒟 ) = ∏ q ∏ P 𝒩 ⁡ ( r q , P , 0 , Σ m ​ ( P , θ ) ) , p ⁡ ( 𝒟 ∣ M m ) = ∫ L m ​ ( θ , 𝒟 ) ​ π m ​ ( 𝑑 θ ) , L_{m}(\theta;\mathcal{D})=\prod_{q}\prod_{P}\ \mathcal{N}\bigl(r_{q,P};\,0,\,\Sigma_{m}(P;\theta)\bigr),\qquad p(\mathcal{D}\mid M_{m})=\int L_{m}(\theta;\mathcal{D})\,\pi_{m}(d\theta), over training queries q q and training pools P P , so a single ( q , P ) (q,P) pair is one term and the factorisation needs defending on both indices. Overlapping pools can reuse observations in the product likelihood. We limit pairwise Jaccard overlap to reduce this reuse, but the resulting pools are not independent. It was violated in an earlier version of these experiments: a BFS ball of the requested size is the entire giant component on the small graphs, so the twelve training pools had mean pairwise Jaccard overlap 1.000 1.000 on texas and cornell and 0.898 0.898 on wisconsin , and identical data was entering the evidence twelve times. Training pools are now accepted only when they overlap every previously accepted one by less than 0.25 0.25 , which yields twelve pools on cora , citeseer and film and exactly one on the three small graphs. These are near-disjoint rather than independent, and we describe them that way throughout. We note it as a limitation of the evidence calculation. We report the corresponding sensitivity check. Bayesian Residual Propagation under Covariance Uncertainty Robert Richardson Affiliation: Department of Statistics, Brigham Young University Email: richardson@stat.byu.edu Abstract Observing a prediction error at one node can help correct predictions elsewhere, but the benefit depends on the residual dependence between nodes. A graph suggests where that dependence might occur, yet does not establish its sign or strength. We develop a Bayesian model of residual covariance to determine how revealed errors should update a fixed feature-based predictor. For a fixed set of revealed nodes, we derive an exact identity for the change in expected squared error under linear residual propagation. The identity characterizes the optimal linear update and expresses the excess error of any other update as an exact quadratic. Under covariance uncertainty, the Bayes-optimal fixed linear update uses the posterior mean covariance. We average over four positive-semidefinite covariance families representing no dependence, positive dependence, negative dependence, and dependence whose sign can alternate with graph distance. Across eight graph benchmarks, four show posterior support within the distance-profile family for negative covariance between neighbors and alternating signs with distance. Among the evaluated methods, ours achieves the smallest worst-case recall gap to the best method on each graph. The method improves squared error over residual propagation on five of eight graphs, but performs substantially worse on one dense heterophilous graph. In these experiments, selecting the highest-posterior family performs similarly to model averaging. 1 Introduction We consider prediction on a graph when a feature-based predictor is available and only some node labels can be observed. For each query, the task is to predict which nodes are relevant. Each observed label reveals a prediction error that may help correct predictions at other nodes. An error at one node may call for an adjustment in the same direction elsewhere, an adjustment in the opposite direction, or no adjustment. The graph alone does not tell us which response is appropriate or how large the adjustment should be. We use the graph to construct candidate models of residual covariance, allowing positive, negative, and sign-changing dependence. We learn a posterior over these models from previously labelled queries. For a new query, the resulting covariance estimate guides both the selection of nodes for labelling and the updates to predictions after their labels are observed. Contributions. First, for centred residuals and a fixed set of revealed nodes, we derive an exact identity for the reduction in expected squared error under linear propagation. The identity gives the optimal linear update and expresses the excess error of any other update as an exact quadratic. For a single revealed node, any nonzero adjustment increases expected error when the true residual covariance with the target node is zero. A positive propagation coefficient also increases expected squared error when that covariance is negative. Second, we derive a Bayesian rule for propagation when the residual covariance is unknown. Under expected squared-error loss, the optimal linear rule with coefficients fixed before observing the new labels uses the posterior mean residual covariance. For a single reveal, the adjustment coefficient is zero exactly when the posterior mean cross-covariance is zero, so no separate threshold is needed to turn propagation off. Third, we construct four positive-semidefinite covariance families representing no residual dependence, positive dependence, negative dependence, and dependence whose sign can alternate with graph distance. Proposition 1 shows that the standard Laplacian covariance model considered here has nonnegative covariance entries and nonnegative propagation coefficients. It therefore cannot represent negative residual covariance or covariance that alternates in sign with graph distance. We evaluate the resulting propagation decisions on eight graph benchmarks with varying levels of homophily. 1.1 Relation to prior work Our work builds on residual propagation and methods for learning on heterophilous graphs. Residual propagation. Previous work has shown that residuals from feature-based predictors can retain graph structure and that propagating these residuals can improve predictions. Jia and Benson (2020) model GNN regression residuals with a graph-structured Gaussian distribution and estimate a signed dependence parameter by marginal likelihood. Their full model therefore allows both positive and negative residual correlation. Their lightweight LP-GNN variant and the correction step of Huang et al. (2021) assume positive residual dependence. Our experiments include Laplacian propagation and the correction step of Huang et al. (2021) as baselines. They do not include Jia and Benson’s learned signed model. Our method instead places a posterior over several covariance families, including a null model and a distance-based family that permits uniformly negative or alternating covariance across positive graph distances. We hold the feature-based predictor fixed and use the inferred covariance to update its predictions. Heterophily and selective propagation. Methods that encourage neighbouring nodes to agree can perform poorly on heterophilous graphs, where connected nodes often have different labels ( Pei et al., 2020 ; Zhu et al., 2020 ; Lim et al., 2021 ) . Choi et al. (2025) address uncertainty about edges with an adaptive method that can block propagation. Other methods allow propagation to adapt to the graph: FAGCN combines low- and high-frequency components using weights that can be negative ( Bo et al., 2021 ) , while GPR-GNN learns signed polynomial coefficients ( Chien et al., 2021 ) . These two methods learn their propagation weights as part of training the predictor. We hold the feature-based predictor fixed and use residuals from previously labelled queries to infer which covariance structures are supported by the data. The resulting posterior determines how newly observed errors update the remaining predictions. Label heterophily alone does not determine the residual dependence that remains after fitting the predictor. Our distinction. We focus on uncertainty about graph-based residual covariance and its consequences for propagation. The update has the standard Bayes-linear form ( Goldstein and Wooff, 2007 ) .
